parts.text:
24 A vehicle carries a microwave transmitter that emits microwaves of a constant frequency. A
stationary observer has a microwave receiver.
The vehicle moves directly towards the observer at constant speed. The observer detects
microwaves of frequency Fo.
The vehicle then accelerates, still moving towards the observer, travels at higher steady speed
for a time and then decelerates until it stops.
What is the variation in the frequency of the microwaves that are detected by the observer?
A
The observed frequency will fall, then remain steady then return to the frequency Fo.
B
The observed frequency will fall, then remain steady then rise to a higher frequency than Fo.
C
The observed frequency will rise, then remain steady then fall to a lower frequency than Fo.
D
The observed frequency will rise, then remain steady then return to the frequency Fo.

hints: Notice the vehicle is moving directly towards the stationary observer, so each new wavefront is emitted closer to the observer and the observed wavelength is shortened.
Recall that for sound and microwaves a faster speed of approach gives a shorter observed wavelength and, with $f = v/\lambda$, a larger increase in observed frequency.
Compare the starting motion at constant speed giving $F_o$ with the final state where the vehicle stops, where there is no Doppler shift and the observer receives the lower emitted frequency.
walkthrough: Identify the start: the vehicle approaches at constant speed, so the observer receives a Doppler-shifted frequency $F_o$ that is higher than the constant emitted frequency.

State the rule: motion towards the observer crowds wavefronts together, giving $\lambda_{obs} < \lambda_{emitted}$ and $f_{obs} = v/\lambda_{obs} > f_{emitted}$, with larger approach speed giving larger $f_{obs}$.
Apply the acceleration phase: speed towards the observer increases, so $\lambda_{obs}$ shortens further and the detected frequency rises above $F_o$.
Apply the higher steady speed phase: speed is constant but larger than at the start, so the detected frequency remains steady at a value above $F_o$.
Apply the deceleration to stop: speed towards the observer falls to zero, so $\lambda_{obs}$ lengthens back to $\lambda_{emitted}$ and the detected frequency falls continuously.
Compare the end to the start: when stopped there is no Doppler shift, so the final frequency is the emitted frequency, which is lower than the approaching frequency $F_o$. This is option C.

A.explanation: A source approaching the observer cannot give a fall in frequency, as the observed wavelength is shortened and $f_o = v/\lambda_{obs}$ is increased.

B.explanation: The first part is wrong because accelerating towards the observer increases the Doppler blueshift, so frequency must rise above $F_o$, not fall.

C.explanation: Faster approach gives larger blueshift then steady high frequency, and stopping removes the blueshift so final frequency equals the emitted frequency which is below $F_o$.

D.explanation: The rise then steady part is correct, but the final stopped source has zero Doppler shift so the frequency must fall below the approaching value $F_o$, not return to $F_o$.
